title: 683529758557/541NV17: Franco & Sons Savoy Restaurant 8, Chester Street, Mold, CH7 1EG
text:
TRIBIWNLYS PRISIO CYMRU - VALUATION TRIBUNAL FOR WALES

Non-Domestic Rating Decision

Page 1 of 3
Appellant: Mr Guiseppe M Franco (Occupier)

Appellant’s Address: Franco & Sons Savoy Restaurant, 8 Chester Street,
Mold, Flintshire CH7 1EG

Appeal number: 683529758557/192NV17/40

The Matter Appealed against: 2017 Rating List

Date of Hearing: Wednesday 15 May 2019

Appearances:  Mrs M O’Connor for the respondent Valuation Officer

Date of Decision:  23 May 2019

Decision of Tribunal:  Appeal Dismissed

Members of the Tribunal:  Mr P O Williams (Chairperson)
Mrs J Angell
Mr W P Bagnall

Tribunal Clerk: Mrs C Jones

Introduction:

1. Mr Franco made a proposal to alter an entry in the 2017 Non-Domestic
Rating List (Rating List) in relation to the appeal hereditament, restaurant
and premises, 8 Chester Street, Mold.  The Valuation Officer (VO)
received the proposal on 20 September 2017 and in making his proposal,
the appellant sought a reduction in the appeal hereditament’s entry in the
Rating List with effect from the 1 April 2017.

2. The Clerk reported that prior to the hearing the appellant had asked that
his appeal be heard in his absence as he was unable to attend.

3. The following is a summary of the case and is not intended to be an
exhaustive record of the proceedings. However, the parties can be
assured that all the evidence was fully considered by the Tribunal when it
arrived at its decision. Consequently, the absence of reference to any
statement, or evidence, should not be construed as being overlooked.

Summary of the Case

4. The VO told the Tribunal that the appeal property was a restaurant located
midway on Chester Street, just off the main High Street in Mold.  The
property comprised of a ground floor café and restaurant, valued on a
zoning basis adopting a price per m2 of £245.

Non-Domestic Rating Decision

Page 2 of 3
5. The VO had inspected the property on the 1 May 2019 and had
discussions with Mr Franco.  She stated that the appellant had noted that
since the valuation list was compiled many shops had closed in the town
centre which in his opinion effected the Rateable Value (RV).  She had
advised the appellant that this would have to be dealt with on a separate
appeal under the grounds of a material change of circumstances, as the
current appeal was against the compiled list entry.

6. The VO stated that Mr Franco’s main contention was that the appeal
property hadn’t changed since the original valuation was carried out and
therefore his RV should not be increased.  He also contended that there
was nothing on his street to attract people to his business.

7. It was explained that the tone adopted for Chester Street was £245m2 and
£285m2, the shops closer to the High Street adopting £285.  The VO had
explained the basis of valuation and how the VOA arrived at the price per
meter squared and discussed the evidence with Mr Franco.  The VO
believed that this evidence fully supported the current tone of £245m2 that
was adopted.

10. In conclusion of her evidence, Mrs O’Connor stated that in light of the
supporting evidence which fully supported the current price of £245m2, she
requested the appeal be dismissed.

11. At the conclusion of the hearing, the Tribunal decided to reserve its
decision.

Reasons for Decision

12. Having considered all the evidence placed before it, the Tribunal decided
to dismiss the appeal.  In arriving at its decision, the Tribunal gave the
following reasons.

13. It made its decision having regard to the prevailing legislation: Schedule 6
of the Local Government Finance Act 1988.

14. The Tribunal considered whether the evidence presented to it would
justify a reduction in the rateable value of the appeal property.  It must
consider the hypothetical tenants rental bid, looking at the property vacant
and to let.

15. Looking at the rental summary provided by the Valuation Officer the
Tribunal was happy that the tone of £245m2 applied was reasonable. It
accepted that the appeal property’s rateable value was in line with other
similar properties in the locality.

16. The Tribunal felt that the settlements quoted by the Valuation Officer,
demonstrated that there was an accepted tone for properties on Chester
Street.

17. The onus is on the appellant to prosecute the case.  The appellant
provided no contrary rental evidence or information in support of his
contention for a reduction in the rateable value.

18. Although the Tribunal was sympathetic to the plight of the appellant and
appreciated the tough trading conditions faced in the area, it did not
believe that any hard evidence had been provided to justify a reduction in
the property’s rateable value.
